frameworks.name: Three-Channel Contractor Sourcing Framework
frameworks.definition: A ranked hierarchy of three platforms for sourcing cheap labor contractors (Google My Business low-review listings, Facebook Marketplace, Nextdoor), plus an SMS-blast mega-channel that outperforms all three on speed and volume.

claims.text: In a drop-servicing model (generating leads and contracting the work to third parties), Google My Business listings with low review counts signal contractors who are actively seeking business but receiving little organic demand, making them more receptive to commission-split arrangements than established high-review competitors.
claims.speaker: Ericvelch
conditions: Drop-servicing / lead-generation model where operator does not perform the work personally
Local service categories (e.g., plumbing, cleaning, car detailing)
claims.mechanism: Low review count indicates the business is not attracting customers organically; hunger for work lowers the resistance to accepting a lead-generation commission split.
bounded_by: Contractors with many reviews and high demand are unlikely to accept low commission splits
Listings that appear to be pure SEO pages (no real business behind them) waste contact effort

claims.text: For drop-servicing operators sourcing contractors on Google My Business, a minimum rating threshold of 4.7 stars filters out poor-quality service providers while still targeting contractors who lack enough volume to be resistant to commission arrangements.
claims.speaker: Ericvelch
conditions: Service quality matters to the operator's downstream clients
Local service businesses (plumbing, cleaning, detailing)

numbers.axis: Google Business Profile star rating as a proxy for contractor quality

bounded_by: Rating alone does not confirm reliability; test with one job before full onboarding

claims.text: Facebook Marketplace suppliers price themselves below market rates — sometimes under $100 for a car detail — because the platform's desperation dynamic attracts workers who urgently need income and are down-pricing themselves to win any work at all.
claims.speaker: Ericvelch
conditions: Local service labor sourcing
Low-to-mid ticket service categories (detailing, cleaning, basic trades)
claims.mechanism: Marketplace participants self-select by willingness to market on a channel associated with distressed sellers; price-sensitivity and urgency are correlated with platform choice.
bounded_by: Higher-ticket trades (plumbing) may attract contractors who expect better-than-marketplace rates

claims.text: Sending an SMS blast using Outscraper-scraped GMB phone numbers loaded into a CRM (e.g., Go High Level) produces hundreds of contractor responses faster than manual platform outreach across Google My Business, Facebook Marketplace, and Nextdoor combined.
claims.speaker: Ericvelch
conditions: Drop-servicing operator seeking to recruit multiple contractors simultaneously
Local service categories with high GMB listing density (plumbing, cleaning, detailing)
claims.mechanism: Outscraper scrapes every GMB listing for a given category and city into a contact list; mass SMS delivery reaches the full universe of listed contractors in a single send rather than one-by-one manual outreach.
bounded_by: Receiving hundreds of responses creates its own management burden; operators must filter and handpick
Go High Level requires phone number verification and has messaging costs; Dialpad is a free alternative but requires manual setup

claims.text: Routing contractor SMS blast responses to a secondary phone number (not the operator's personal cell) filters for higher-commitment respondents because taking the step of messaging a different number signals greater interest, while also preventing the operator's personal cell from being flooded with incoming calls.
claims.speaker: Ericvelch
conditions: After sending a mass SMS blast to contractors
Operator does not want personal phone overwhelmed
claims.mechanism: Extra friction (switching to a second number) self-selects for motivated respondents; those who call the personal cell directly rather than the funneled number represent lower-quality leads who did not follow instructions.

claims.text: An Outscraper scrape of all GMB-listed contractors in a category for one city costs approximately $10 (initial deposit) and does not require repeated payment if the card is removed before auto-billing, making the full contact list essentially a one-time $10 acquisition.
claims.speaker: Ericvelch
conditions: Operator removes payment card after initial deposit before auto-billing triggers

numbers.axis: Cost to acquire a city-wide contractor contact list via Outscraper GMB scrape

anchors.region: Auto-billing if card left on file
Cost if card removed after deposit

bounded_by: Accuracy of Outscraper data depends on GMB listing completeness in that category/city

claims.text: The total all-in cost to execute a contractor-sourcing SMS blast (Outscraper data + CRM SMS credits) is approximately $100-$150, which the operator asserts is worth it for the time saved versus purely manual platform outreach.
claims.speaker: Ericvelch
conditions: Single city, single service category
Using Go High Level or equivalent CRM for SMS delivery

numbers.axis: All-in cost of the SMS blast contractor-sourcing method

bounded_by: Does not include ongoing CRM subscription cost
Manual platform outreach (GMB, Facebook, Nextdoor) has near-zero direct cost but higher time cost

claims.text: In drop-servicing commission arrangements for higher-ticket trades (e.g., plumbing), operators should withhold the commission percentage from the SMS blast message and reveal it only on a follow-up call, because disclosing 40% upfront triggers resistance before the operator can frame the value they provide (marketing, booking, customer management).
claims.speaker: Ericvelch
conditions: Higher-ticket service categories where contractors will scrutinize split percentages
Commission split is 40% to operator / 60% to contractor
claims.mechanism: Revealing commission percentage on the call allows the operator to simultaneously explain the value exchange (marketing effort, lead volume, customer management), reducing resistance compared to a cold bare-percentage disclosure.

numbers.axis: Commission split percentage kept by operator vs. contractor in drop-servicing arrangement

bounded_by: For lower-ticket categories (car detailing), the commission rate can be included in the SMS and even in a Google Form without a follow-up call, because stakes are lower and volume matters more than individual negotiation

claims.text: For low-ticket, low-barrier service categories (e.g., car detailing), a Google Form embedded in the SMS blast can replace the phone-call vetting step entirely: the operator collected 20 contractor sign-ups in one city at 50% commission with no follow-up calls.
claims.speaker: Ericvelch
conditions: Low-ticket service category with minimal skill or liability requirements
Operator includes pricing and commission terms directly in the SMS form

numbers.axis: Contractor sign-ups from a single SMS-blast Google Form campaign for car detailing

bounded_by: Does not apply to higher-ticket trades where contractor vetting and trust-building require a call

claims.text: Before fully onboarding a contractor, drop-servicing operators should send 1-3 test jobs to verify the contractor correctly reports job amounts and passes the correct commission share, using a customer check-in call (framed as being for tax purposes) to confirm the total charged matches the contractor's reported figure.
claims.speaker: Ericvelch
conditions: Drop-servicing arrangement where the contractor quotes or invoices directly
Operator cannot be on-site to verify job completion price
claims.mechanism: Contractors who quote jobs directly have opportunity to under-report to the operator; a post-job customer check-in surfaces any discrepancy between what the customer paid and what the contractor reported.

numbers.axis: Number of test jobs before full contractor onboarding

anchors.region: Typical test phase before formal onboarding

bounded_by: When the operator does the quoting (fixed-price categories like cleaning or detailing), this verification step is simpler since the operator controls the price before the job
Higher-ticket trades where the contractor quotes on-site require more rigorous verification

claims.text: When vetting contractors from a mass SMS blast response pool, operators should filter for the absence of language barriers and basic professional communication competence, because service contractors who cannot communicate clearly create downstream customer-service problems that fall back on the operator.
claims.speaker: Ericvelch
conditions: Mass SMS blast has produced a large pool of respondents
Operator will be acting as intermediary between client and contractor

claims.text: Higher-ticket service niches (e.g., plumbing) require a more structured contractor onboarding process — phone vetting call, written expectations, invoicing system integration — whereas lower-ticket categories (e.g., car detailing) can be onboarded with lighter process because individual job risk and client expectation are lower.
claims.speaker: Ericvelch
conditions: Drop-servicing model with contractors performing work
Operator acting as lead generator and account manager

examples.text: The speaker described an example where he ran an SMS blast for car detailers in his city. Rather than following up individually, he embedded a Google Form directly in the SMS asking interested contractors to fill in their details and pricing preferences. Approximately 20 detailers completed the form, each agreeing to do jobs for 50% of the job price, giving him an instant bench of 20 contractors in one city at no cost beyond the initial data acquisition. He contrasted this with plumbing, where the higher stakes require actual phone calls and structured onboarding before trusting a contractor with a client job.

The speaker showed a GTA-area plumber GMB listing with one review as an example of the target profile: visibly in business (products listed, service name in title), clearly seeking work, but receiving almost no organic GMB-driven customers. He noted the listing may have been a pure SEO page rather than an active business, illustrating the need to filter for listings that are definitely active operations rather than abandoned or template-built profiles.

The speaker showed a message thread on Facebook Marketplace with a plumber he had contacted. The exchange demonstrated the minimal friction of the initial approach: send a message, get their phone number, call them briefly. He noted car detailers on the same platform were listing services for under $100, illustrating how the desperation dynamic of marketplace participants drives prices well below conventional rates.

practices.text: When messaging contractors on GMB or Facebook Marketplace for a drop-servicing commission arrangement, call rather than message where possible — phone contact establishes rapport faster and removes ambiguity about your offer versus getting lost in a message queue.

After a contractor passes the test-job phase, schedule a longer onboarding call to attach them to your invoicing system, communicate your expectations list, and clarify what you will and will not handle — use ChatGPT to draft the expectations document if needed.

Keep the initial SMS blast message short and specific: state the approximate lead volume you are offering (e.g., 10-15 plumbing leads per day), identify yourself as a local company, say you are looking for someone to contract the work, and direct responses to a secondary number rather than your personal cell.

After a contractor completes a job they quoted on-site, call the customer and frame it as a check-in for tax purposes to confirm the total amount charged — this surfaces any under-reporting by the contractor before it becomes a pattern.
